soil-chem-041.title: The hidden costs of watering dry land
soil-chem-041.text: Irrigated land covers about 16% of the world's agricultural area but grows roughly 40% of its total harvest. That harvest has a price. The environmental impact of irrigation covers the changes it makes to the quantity and quality of soil and water. It also covers their effects on nature and society in river basins and downstream. Direct effects include reduced river flow downstream, more evaporation in the irrigated area and a rising water table from increased groundwater recharge. Slower but longer-lasting effects follow: waterlogging, salination, ecological damage and socioeconomic impacts. Deep percolation losses are commonly 40% to 60%, raising water tables. Where tables are shallow, less water is applied, the soil is no longer leached and salinity develops. Over-irrigation causes {{ref:soil-chem-010}} through rising water tables, while under-irrigation fails to flush salts out. About one-third of irrigated land in the major irrigation countries is or soon will be badly salt-affected. Estimates run 13% in Israel, 15% in China, 20% in Australia, 30% in Egypt and 50% in Iraq. Pumping wells beyond recharge mines groundwater and can make the land sink and, on coasts, saltwater intrusion. Stagnant water tables at the surface also raise the incidence of water-borne diseases such as malaria and schistosomiasis.

soil-chem-035.title: Calcareous soils, built on chalk and limestone
soil-chem-035.text: Soils formed on limestone or chalk lean alkaline, and the reason is simple chemistry. A calcareous soil is one formed from or containing a high proportion of calcium carbonate, as calcite or aragonite. The carbonate ion is a base, so soils whose parent material contains it are relatively alkaline. They may have a calcic horizon, a layer of secondary carbonates. It holds above 15% {{ref:soil-fert-060}} and at least 5% more carbonate than the layer below. {{ref:soil-class-086}} grows on soils rich in calcium carbonate from underlying chalk or limestone. Calcisols are common on calcareous parent materials in arid and semi-arid environments, and loess is often calcareous. In such low-acidity soils, earthworms mix decomposed organic matter into the mineral soil below, forming {{ref:soil-bio-096}}.

soil-chem-036.title: Caliche, the rock that grows inside dry soils
soil-chem-036.text: Where rain is scarce, soil can make its own rock. Caliche is an accumulation of calcium carbonate at depth, where it precipitates and binds other materials such as gravel, sand, clay and silt. Also called calcrete or kankar, it forms layers from a few inches to feet thick, sometimes called a K horizon. Root carbon dioxide in the A horizon, up to 15 times atmospheric levels, dissolves calcium carbonate as bicarbonate. In the less active B horizon below, it reverts to carbonate. Caliche forms where annual precipitation is under 65 centimeters and mean annual temperature exceeds 5 °C. Wetter climates leach the calcium away. Its depth follows rainfall: about 25 centimeters down at 35 centimeters of rain a year, about 125 centimeters at 75, and gone above 100. It occurs worldwide in dry-region soils, from central and western Australia to the Kalahari and the High Plains of the western United States. Deposition takes several thousand years, and the calcium can arrive as windblown dust even over calcium-poor bedrock. Impermeable caliche blocks drainage and roots, and the basic soil it creates can cause iron deficiency that yellows the youngest leaves. Caliches store significant carbon, and calcretes in the geologic record preserve past climates.

soil-chem-038.title: Gypcrust, the gypsum armor of the driest lands
soil-chem-038.text: Where it is too dry even for calcrete, gypsum takes over. A gypcrust is a hardened soil layer made of around 95% gypsum, calcium sulfate. It is the arid-climate counterpart of calcrete, which cannot form in very arid climates. Gypcrust horizons can be up to 5 m thick with 75–97% gypsum. They form mostly where annual rainfall averages under 250 mm, since gypsum is moderately soluble and leaches under higher rainfall. Formation runs in three stages: crystallization from surface brines or groundwater, transport and redeposition by wind or water, and alteration above or below the capillary fringe. Gypsum cements are rarely as strong as calcretes or silcretes, though gypcrete has been used for road construction in the Sahara.

soil-chem-014.title: Drains that pull salt and water away
soil-chem-014.text: In many cases, a water table 0.6 to 0.8 m down, as a seasonal average, is deep enough. Drainage for salinity control carries salty water away and lowers the water table, usually with horizontal systems but also with vertical ones. A fluctuating water table helps the soil breathe, expelling root carbon dioxide and drawing in oxygen. A water table that is not too deep also discourages over-irrigation, since crop yields would fall as it rose. Where wet and dry seasons are marked, running drains only in the wet season saves irrigation water. This is called controlled drainage.

soil-chem-013.title: Leaching requirement: the water it takes to hold salt down
soil-chem-013.text: The leaching requirement is the amount that must percolate through the root zone to hold soil salinity at a desired level, worked out from the salt balance. That desired level depends on the crop's tolerance to salt. The calculation rests on the water balance of the zone above the water table. It sets infiltration of rain and irrigation against evaporation, percolation to groundwater and capillary rise. Leaching efficiency is often 0.7 to 0.8 but can be lower in poorly structured heavy clays. In Portugal's Leziria Grande it was only 0.15. From the requirement, the irrigation and drainage needed for salinity control can be computed.

soil-chem-016.title: Computer models that forecast salt in fields
soil-chem-016.text: Soil salinity models are computer models of water and salt movement in soil, used to predict salinity under irrigation and drainage. Most, such as SWAP, DrainMod-S, UnSatChem and Hydrus, pair two equations. Richards' equation handles unsaturated water flow, and Fick's convection–diffusion equation handles the salts. These models need hard-to-measure soil properties, short time steps and daily or hourly data. They are also hard to calibrate, because field salinity varies greatly. Simpler models such as SaltMod use monthly or seasonal water and salt balances for long-term predictions, and {{ref:soil-chem-040}} adds spatial variation with groundwater.

soil-chem-015.title: Sacrificing strips of land to save the rest
soil-chem-015.text: One way to beat salt is to surrender some land to it. In strip cropping for salinity control, alternate strips are irrigated and those between are never planted. The irrigated strips have a higher water table, which pushes groundwater toward the unirrigated ones. That flow acts as subsurface drainage and lets the cropped strips leach. In the dry, sacrificial strips, groundwater rises by capillarity and evaporates, leaving its salts behind, so these strips salinize. They need not be wasted. They can carry livestock, salt-resistant grasses or deep-rooted salt-tolerant trees such as Casuarina, Eucalyptus or Atriplex, or be used for salt harvesting.

soil-chem-037.title: Chile's nitrate-rich caliche of the Atacama
soil-chem-037.text: Chile's Atacama Desert holds vast deposits also called caliche, though they are not the carbonate layers of {{ref:soil-chem-036}}. They mix gypsum, sodium chloride, other salts and sand with nitrate minerals called salitre, which is sodium and potassium nitrate. The deposits average 7.5% sodium nitrate, with sodium sulfate, sodium chloride, borate, iodine and perchlorate. Salitre earned Chile important export revenue until the early 1930s, when Europe began making nitrates industrially in large quantities. Caliche is also Chile's main iodine ore, and the country hosts over half the world's iodine reserves. Its origin is unclear. An evaporated prehistoric inland sea and weathering of the Andes have both been proposed.

soil-chem-040.title: SahysMod, a salt forecaster for field engineers
soil-chem-040.text: SahysMod was designed for field technicians, engineers and planners rather than specialized geohydrologists. Developed by the land-improvement institute ILRI, the program predicts the salinity of soil moisture, groundwater and drainage water in irrigated land. It also predicts water table depth and drain discharge. It maps spatial variation with a network of polygons, up to 240 internal and 120 external. Groundwater levels and flows between polygons come from numerically solving the Boussinesq equation. The program runs on seasonal inputs and outputs, with one to four seasons a year. Salt balances are computed for each soil reservoir separately, and farmers' responses to waterlogging and salinity can be built in.

soil-chem-045.title: Halophytes, the plants that thrive on salt
soil-chem-045.text: Beans and rice tolerate irrigation water with about 1–3 g/L of dissolved solids, and barley and date palm about 5 g/L. Salicornia bigelovii grows well at 70 g/L. It is a halophyte, a salt-tolerant plant that grows in soils or waters of high salinity, such as salt marshes, mangroves and saline semi-deserts. Perhaps only 2% of plant species are halophytes. Most are glycophytes, which high salinity damages fairly easily. In 1936 Iversen grouped halophytes by soil NaCl: oligo-halophytes at 0.01 to 0.1%, meso-halophytes at 0.1 to 1%, and euhalophytes above 1%. Some, such as Suaeda salsa, store salt ions taken from soil. They can lower soil salinity enough for glycophytes to grow again.

soil-chem-042.title: Framboids, the microscopic raspberries of pyrite
soil-chem-042.text: Under a microscope, some pyrite looks like a raspberry. A framboid is a roughly spherical cluster of tiny crystals, common in some sedimentary minerals, especially pyrite. Clusters average 5–20 μm across and are built of regular microcrystals around 0.5 μm in diameter. Rust first used the name in 1935, from the French framboise, raspberry. In {{ref:soil-chem-030}}, bacteria such as Desulfovibrio desulfuricans reduce sulfate to hydrogen sulfide. It reacts with ferrous iron to form fine, highly reactive framboidal pyrite. This pyrite is common in coastal sediments of marshes, estuaries and beaches, and greigite is considered an essential precursor. Framboids were once thought to be fossil bacterial colonies. They have since been made in the laboratory and found in places hostile to microbial life.

soil-chem-026.title: Keeping water out of salty groundwater
soil-chem-026.text: The drier a soil enters winter, the more water it can store instead of leaking it to groundwater. Soils take up water according to their field capacity and starting dryness. Managing dryland salinity builds on that. It means cutting groundwater recharge through soils and vegetation, and coping with salt where groundwater discharges. Returning recharge to pre-clearing levels is usually infeasible, because too few profitable perennials can replace crops. The aim is to minimize it instead, with alley farming, perennials and leaf cover through winter and spring. In discharge areas, salinity is managed with salt-tolerant plants or with engineering such as deep open drains, pumps and siphons. There is a trade-off, since recharge is also the source of fresh groundwater.

soil-chem-025.title: Natural salt and the salt people make
soil-chem-025.text: Not all salty land is a human failure. Salinity divides into primary salinity, which is natural, and secondary salinity, which human activity induces. Primary salinity occurs naturally in arid and saline settings such as salt lakes, marshes, pans and salt flats. Past cycles of drainage, desiccation and sea winds left it there. Secondary salinity results directly from development, agriculture and irrigation, and it harms biodiversity and land productivity. Secondary salinization can also make soils dispersive, so excess salt needs managing at landscape scale.

soil-chem-027.title: Saline seeps, where salty groundwater surfaces
soil-chem-027.text: Crusts of alkali salt crystals mark a saline seep, a place where salty water reaches the surface and evaporates. Seeps form by capillary rise from a water table below the surface, or where a water table flows out at the surface. Saline discharge areas are called seeps where groundwater meets the soil surface, and scalds where water is lost by evaporation only. They harm agriculture by reducing yields and restricting growth. Yet they also host salt-adapted and often endemic organisms.

soil-chem-031.title: How drained pyrite turns into sulfuric acid
soil-chem-031.text: Let air reach pyrite in a drained soil, and the mineral becomes acid. The overall reaction is 4FeS2 + 15O2 + 14H2O → 16H+ + 8SO42− + 4Fe(OH)3. It yields sulfuric acid and iron(III) hydroxide, and it can make the soil extremely acidic. The orange iron(III) hydroxide precipitates and locks up the alkalinity, while the acidity stays active as sulfuric acid. That acidity frees large amounts of Al3+ from clay minerals, harmful to vegetation. It leaves behind hydrogen clay, which is stable but poor in nutrients. Other products include hydrogen sulfide, sulfur, hematite, goethite and iron sulfates such as jarosite. So these soils range in color from black and blue-gray to red, orange and yellow.

soil-chem-033.title: Acid base accounting: balancing a soil's acid books
soil-chem-033.text: How much lime does a load of dug-up or dredged sulfidic material need to neutralize it? Acid base accounting answers questions like that. It quantifies the sources of acidity and alkalinity in acid sulfate soils so they can be managed. Net acidity is potential sulfidic acidity plus titratable actual acidity plus retained acidity, minus the acid neutralizing capacity, in mol H+ per tonne of dry soil. Potential sulfidic acidity measures oxidizable reduced inorganic sulfur such as iron sulfides. The chromium reducible sulfur test measures it without interference from sulfate minerals or organic matter. Samples oxidize rapidly in air, so they should be cooled below 4°C at once, and monosulfidic samples frozen.

soil-chem-034.title: Keeping acid sulfate soils wet and safe
soil-chem-034.text: On a Malaysian oil palm estate, drainage was deepened in 1962. Yields fell from 17 tons of fresh fruit per ha in 1960 to 2 in 1965, recovering after the water table was raised in 1966. Managing acid sulfate soils means keeping them wet, restoring their water table or neutralizing their acid, and the estate shows why. Aggressive drainage of potentially acid sulfate soils in the second half of the 20th century had disastrous results: barren land and clear, lifeless water. Where soils cannot be kept wet, surface drainage in rainy periods removes acids formed in dry spells and can reclaim the soil in the long run. When Australia's millennium drought exposed them, a bund, pumping and aerial limestone dosing were used to stop acidification of the Lower Lakes.

soil-chem-032.title: Sulfidic and sulfuric: naming the danger in the mud
soil-chem-032.text: Two words mark the stages of an acid sulfate soil. Sulfidic material holds detectable inorganic sulfides, at least 0.01% sulfidic sulfur in layers at least 30 mm thick. Sulfuric material has a pH below 4 from their oxidation. Sulfidic material splits into hyposulfidic, hypersulfidic and monosulfidic classes. Hypersulfidic material would fall below pH 4 if exposed to oxidizing conditions. Hyposulfidic material would not, though its weathering still yields saline solutions with hazardous metals. Coined mainly by Fanning, Rabenhorst and Fitzpatrick, the terms are diagnostic features in two classification systems, the Australian and the international one. The label 'self-neutralizing' acid sulfate soil is discouraged, because it suggests the soil is not hazardous.

soil-chem-043.title: Maas–Hoffman: the yield line that bends under salt
soil-chem-043.text: Up to a point, salt costs a crop nothing. The Maas–Hoffman model draws crop response to soil salinity as a horizontal line that breaks into a downward slope. The breakpoint, or tolerance, is the salinity up to which yield is unaffected. Beyond it, yield falls. In symbols, yield Y equals the maximum C below the breakpoint Pb, and AX + B above it. Here X is soil salinity, A the slope and B the regression constant. Pb is found by regression and optimization for the best fit. A flat tail in the data, though, can give a misleadingly low breakpoint. An inverted form serves factors such as water table depth, which cut yields only at low values.

soil-chem-018.title: Exchangeable sodium percentage and the swelling of clay
soil-chem-018.text: Clays almost fully saturated with sodium are called bentonite, and they are used to make impermeable curtains below dams. Their exchangeable sodium percentage, or ESP, is near 100%. ESP is the share of a soil's exchangeable cations, and so of its {{ref:soil-chem-046}}, that is sodium. It is calculated as sodium divided by total cations, times 100, and it is a key indicator of dispersive soils. High sodium makes wet particles repel one another. Soils with a high ESP therefore lose structure as their aggregates disperse. Clay with an ESP above 16, in contact with non-saline water, has an expanded double layer, so the soil swells and disperses. Applying gypsum lowers ESP by displacing sodium with calcium.

soil-chem-019.title: Alkali soils, clay ruined by sodium carbonate
soil-chem-019.text: Sodium carbonate is about 78000 times more soluble than calcium carbonate. That gap explains alkali soils: clay soils with a high pH, generally above 8.5, often with poor structure and low infiltration capacity. Na2CO3 can push pH above 8.5, the most that calcium carbonate in equilibrium with dissolved carbon dioxide allows. The sodium carbonate and bicarbonate come from weathering minerals or arrive in irrigation and flood water. As Ca2+ precipitates, clays take up Na+ and their ESP rises. Above an ESP of 16 they swell and disperse, crusting and compacting the topsoil and cutting infiltration. Such soils, also called alkaline sodic soils, often have a hard calcareous layer 0.5 to 1 metre down. Alkalinity is worse in swelling montmorillonite or smectite clays. In principle alkaline soils are not saline, since alkalinity worsens as salinity falls. Rainwater stagnates and evaporates on the surface, so farming is mostly limited to crops tolerant of waterlogging, such as rice. Irrigating with softened water, its calcium and magnesium replaced by sodium, dissolves organic matter and disperses clay, giving the structure typical of alkali soils.

soil-chem-020.title: How people make soils alkaline
soil-chem-020.text: Global sodium chloride consumption reached 280 million tons in 2020. Sodium from industrial and household salts enters surface water and groundwater. Man-made soil alkalinity is alkalinity caused by people, mainly through sodium salts and lime that reach soil in irrigation water, effluent and industrial emissions. Fly ash from coal-fired boilers contains calcium oxide, which dissolves to slaked lime, Ca(OH)2, and water washing off the land carries it into rivers and irrigation systems. Lime softening precipitates Ca2+ and Mg2+ from water and converts its sodium bicarbonate into sodium carbonate. Sodium salt loads are worst downstream in intensively cultivated river basins. There, salts concentrate in the water left after transpiration and evaporation.

soil-chem-022.title: Farming fish on land too salty for crops
soil-chem-022.text: Shrimps, crabs, shellfish and fish such as sea bass and grouper can all be raised in inland saline-alkali water. Saline-alkali aquaculture uses such fish and seafood farming on salty, alkaline land to leach salts, add organic matter and put land unfit for crops to use. Since the 1990s, research and experiments in China and elsewhere have combined agriculture and aquaculture on alkali land with considerable success. China's Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs recommends it as an economically viable and environmentally beneficial way to use saline-alkali land.

soil-chem-023.title: Residual sodium carbonate: rating water's alkali threat
soil-chem-023.text: Water need not be salty to ruin a clay field. The residual sodium carbonate index, or RSC, rates the alkalinity hazard that irrigation water or soil water poses to soil. RSC = (HCO3− + CO32−) − (Ca2+ + Mg2+), in meq/L. For irrigation it should not be much above 1, and preferably below 0.5. It judges water for clay soils with a high cation-exchange capacity. There, sodium high relative to calcium and magnesium makes clay swell or disperse and infiltration collapse. Unlike saline water, high-RSC water does not raise osmotic pressure against root uptake. Yet irrigating clay soils with it creates alkali soils that are left unfarmed. Soda ash from weathered basalt, lime from burnt calcareous coal and industrial soda ash raise river water RSC, often making lower reaches unfit for irrigation.

soil-chem-044.title: Gypsum, the calcium cure for sodium-sick soils
soil-chem-044.text: In the late 18th and early 19th centuries, Nova Scotia gypsum, called plaster, was a sought-after fertilizer for US wheat fields. Agricultural gypsum is calcium sulfate applied to soil as a fertilizer and amendment. It supplies calcium and sulfur without generally changing soil pH. It is used to reclaim saline and sodic soils regardless of pH, lowering the exchangeable sodium percentage. In sodic and acidic soils it turns soluble sodium metaborate into less soluble calcium metaborate, and it reduces aluminium and boron toxicity. It also improves soil structure, water absorption and aeration.

soil-chem-021.title: Reclaiming alkali soils with calcium, acid and drains
soil-chem-021.text: Gypsum does two jobs in an alkali soil. It supplies Ca2+ to replace sodium on the exchange complex, and it turns sodium carbonate into neutral sodium sulfate. Reclaiming alkali soils means supplying calcium or acidifying material to replace or neutralize the excess sodium, then leaching the sodium away. That needs enough natural or artificial subsurface drainage for rain or irrigation water to carry it off. Acidifying minerals such as pyrite, alum or aluminium sulfate, calcium chloride, calcium nitrate and spent acids can also be used. Soils with solid CaCO3 can be reclaimed with grass, compost and other organic waste, which add acidifying material and release CO2 to dissolve calcium. Efforts usually target the top 10 cm, and treatments need repeating in about 5 years as amendments leach or decompose. Halophytes such as glasswort, saltwort or barilla absorb sodium carbonate into their tissues, a form of plant-based cleanup, and their ash yields soda. Saline soils are a different case. They are mostly also sodic but keep good structure, so leaching does not usually turn them into alkali soils, and they mostly need no gypsum.

reviews.acidity-alkalinity-and-salinity: Acid, salt and sodium are three different troubles, and this chapter has followed each from cause to cure. Acidification comes from acid rain, ammonium fertilizers, roots and oxidizing pyrite, and lime is the main remedy. Salinity rises wherever evaporation leaves dissolved salts behind, whether irrigation water brings them or cleared land lets groundwater lift them, and leaching water, drains and deep roots carry them back out. Sodium works differently: it disperses clay and blocks infiltration, so indices such as SAR and ESP track it, and gypsum's calcium undoes it. In dry climates the same chemistry builds rock, as calcium carbonate and gypsum harden into caliche and gypcrust.
